blocks.content: EXTREMIST PHASE, SWADESHI, HOME RULE & GANDHIAN TRANSITION

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Partition of Bengal in 1905 by Lord Curzon catalyzed the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement, marking a transition from elite petitioning to mass political action.
Ideological rifts between Moderates and Extremists culminated in the Surat Split of 1907 during the INC session presided over by Rash Behari Ghosh.
The Home Rule League Movement (1916), led separately by Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant, revitalized national politics and popularized the demand for self-government.
The Lucknow Pact (1916) brought unity between the INC's Moderate and Extremist factions and forged a temporary political alliance between the Congress and the Muslim League.
Mahatma Gandhi's arrival and successful local Satyagrahas in Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad (1918), and Kheda (1918) laid the groundwork for mass-based Gandhian nationalism.

blocks.content: 1. Introduction: Transformation of Indian Nationalism (1905–1919)

The period between 1905 and 1919 represents one of the most dynamic and transformative phases of the Indian National Movement. Unlike the earlier Moderate phase (1885–1905), which relied mainly on petitions and constitutional agitation, this phase witnessed the rise of assertive nationalism, mass participation, revolutionary activities, and new political ideas. The movement expanded beyond educated elites and began involving students, women, workers, peasants, and the lower middle class. This era began with the Partition of Bengal in 1905 and culminated in the emergence of Mahatma Gandhi as the central leader of Indian nationalism. For  examinations, this phase is extremely important because questions are repeatedly asked on Swadeshi Movement, Extremists, Surat Split, Home Rule Movement, revolutionary activities, and early Gandhian movements.
2. Partition of Bengal (1905): Causes, Motives and Consequences

In 1905, Lord Curzon announced the Partition of Bengal, dividing it into two provinces – East Bengal and Assam, and West Bengal. Officially, the partition was justified on administrative grounds, citing the large size of Bengal province. However, the real intention behind the partition was political – to weaken the growing nationalist movement in Bengal by dividing the population on communal and regional lines.

• Bengal was the centre of nationalist and revolutionary activities.

• British policy of Divide and Rule aimed to separate Hindus and Muslims.

• Fear of educated Bengali middle class leadership.

• Curtailment of nationalist press and organisations.

The partition was widely opposed across India. Public meetings, protest marches, and boycotts were organised. People realised that constitutional methods had failed, leading to the birth of mass-based movements.
3. Swadeshi and Boycott Movement (1905–1908)

The Swadeshi Movement emerged as a direct reaction to the Partition of Bengal. It aimed at economic self-reliance and national self-respect by boycotting British goods and promoting Indian-made products. This was the first mass movement in Indian history.

• Boycott of foreign cloth, salt, sugar, and other goods.

• Promotion of indigenous industries and handicrafts.

• Establishment of national schools and colleges.

• Use of swadeshi goods in daily life.

• Organisation of strikes, public meetings, and cultural programmes.

The movement spread beyond Bengal to Maharashtra, Punjab, Madras Presidency, and parts of Uttar Pradesh. Students boycotted government schools, women participated in picketing, and workers organised strikes. This marked a shift from elite politics to popular mobilisation.

Achievements:

• Rise of national consciousness.

• Growth of indigenous industries.

• Beginning of mass participation.



Limitations:

• Movement remained regionally concentrated.

• British repression weakened the movement.

• Lack of sustained all-India leadership.
4. Rise of Extremist Nationalism

The Extremists emerged as a response to the failure of Moderate politics. They believed that freedom could not be achieved through petitions but required self-sacrifice, mass struggle, and assertive action.

• Swaraj as an immediate goal.

• Passive resistance and boycott.

• Self-reliance and national education.

• Faith in the strength of the masses.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai were the principal leaders. Tilak popularised nationalism through Ganapati and Shivaji festivals and the slogan ‘Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it’.
5. Surat Split (1907): Causes and Impact

Differences between Moderates and Extremists over methods and leadership culminated in the Surat Split of 1907. The Congress split into two factions, weakening the national movement at a crucial stage.
6. Revolutionary Nationalism (1905–1915)
Some nationalists believed that only armed struggle could overthrow British rule. This gave rise to revolutionary organisations in India and abroad.

7. Home Rule Movement (1916–1918)
The Home Rule Movement aimed at achieving self-government within the British Empire. It marked the revival of nationalist activity after the decline of the Swadeshi Movement.

• Annie Besant launched the Home Rule League in Madras.

• Bal Gangadhar Tilak launched another league in Maharashtra.

• Demand for self-government and political rights.
8. Lucknow Pact (1916): Unity and Compromise
The Lucknow Pact symbolised Hindu-Muslim unity and reunion of Moderates and Extremists. It marked a high point of nationalist unity before the Gandhian era.
9. Entry of Mahatma Gandhi (1917–1918)
Mahatma Gandhi introduced a new form of mass politics based on truth (satya), non-violence (ahimsa), and direct contact with the masses. He transformed the character of the national movement.

• Champaran Satyagraha – Indigo peasants.

• Ahmedabad Mill Strike – Workers’ rights.

• Kheda Satyagraha – Peasant tax relief.
10. British Response: Repression and Reforms

items: Tilak established his Home Rule League at Belgaum in April 1916, whereas Annie Besant launched her league at Adyar (Madras) in September 1916.
Champaran Satyagraha (1917) was Gandhi's first Civil Disobedience, Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918) was his first Hunger Strike, and Kheda (1918) was his first Non-Cooperation movement.
The Surat Split (1907) occurred under the presidency of Rash Behari Ghosh, whereas the reunified Lucknow Session (1916) was presided over by Ambica Charan Mazumdar.

blocks.content: The British responded with repression and limited reforms to control nationalism.

• Morley–Minto Reforms (1909): Separate electorates.

• Montagu Declaration (1917): Promise of responsible government.
11. Significance of the Phase (1905–1919)
This phase transformed Indian nationalism into a mass-based movement, destroyed blind faith in British justice, and prepared the ground for Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience movements.
